Integrations — NetBox, issue trackers and your own Python

Wire SATOM to systems it does not own — NetBox maintenance windows, Jira / OpenProject / Vikunja change tickets, and small Python hooks that run on SATOM events in a sandboxed runner.

👤 ForAdministratorAdvanced user
🔑 Permissionsusers.manage
📍 WhereSettings → System → Integrations (URL /settings/integrations/)

What is it?#

Settings → Integrations is where SATOM connects to systems it does not own:

  • NetBox — records the maintenance window of a change request on the NetBox object of each appliance, and keeps a map of which NetBox object each appliance is.
  • Issue tracker — opens a real ticket in Jira Cloud, OpenProject or Vikunja when you raise the ticket for a change request.
  • Confluence — the connections the Wiki publishes articles through; the space and the parent page are picked on each article (see Wiki → Confluence).
  • Integration hooks — your own small Python scripts, run on SATOM events (a change requested or approved, a window opening or closing, an upgrade finished or failed, an alert fired) by a separate, unprivileged runner.

Everything here is optional and outbound. With all of it off, change requests and upgrades work unchanged.

What does it do?#

  • Tests each connection on demand and reports the measured round-trip time.
  • Stores tokens encrypted (hook secrets in the vault when one is configured) and never shows them again.
  • Opens and closes NetBox maintenance windows for change requests.
  • Opens exactly one tracker ticket per change request.
  • Queues hooks to a runner that executes them out of the web process, with a hard timeout and only the secrets they declare.
  • Lists every hook run with its status, duration and redacted output.

Requirements#

  • users.manage.
  • Network reachability from the SATOM node to NetBox / the tracker.
  • For hooks: satom-integrations.path enabled on every node that serves the web console (see Advanced).

Permissions#

Every page, button and endpoint here requires users.manage (Administrator). Without it the Integrations entry is not shown in the Settings menu and the URLs answer 403. Driving a change request (raising the ticket, opening the NetBox window) also requires users.manage.

How to use#

Connect NetBox#

  1. In the NetBox card tick Enabled, enter the Base URL (https://netbox.example.com) and the API token ("Stored encrypted. Leaving this blank keeps the existing token — it never clears it.").
  2. Set Timeout (s) (1–60) and Verify TLS.
  3. Choose the Maintenance-window backend (table below) and Save.
  4. Press Test connection. It reports Connected to NetBox and the elapsed milliseconds, or the reason it failed.
Backend What it writes Trade-off
Journal entry (default) A journal entry on the object with the change id, window and reason; closing adds a second entry Full history; journal entries are not filterable in NetBox
Object tag Adds the maint-window tag (created if absent); removes it on close Filterable; records that a window exists, not which or when
Object custom fields Sets maint_window_start / maint_window_end Structured and filterable, but both custom fields must already exist for that object type (device or virtual machine); SATOM names the missing ones

Map appliances to NetBox objects#

  1. In Device mapping, enter for each appliance its NetBox object: a device id on its own (7) or a virtual machine with its prefix (vm:95). The same number is a different object in the two types.
  2. Leave a row blank to fall back to an exact, case-sensitive name match — devices first, then virtual machines. The Resolution column shows mapped or by name.
  3. Press Save mapping.

Scheduled reconciliation fills the map for you: set Task name, Appliances per round (1–500, default 25), Runs daily at a time (default 03:00) or every n minutes/hours/days, tick enabled and save. This creates or updates one netbox_reconcile row on System Automations. Each round asks NetBox about unmapped appliances, lowest id first, and writes the ones it finds by name as explicit ids. It creates nothing in NetBox and never removes a mapping you wrote.

Connect an issue tracker#

  1. In Issue tracker pick the backend, fill in the URL, token and the fields below, and Save. Tick Clear the stored token to remove a token; leaving the box blank keeps it.
  2. Press Test connection. It authenticates and fetches the configured project, so a token that cannot see the project fails here, not during a change window.
Backend Authentication Project field Notes
Jira Cloud Account e-mail + API token (Atlassian account → Security → API tokens) Project key (the prefix in OPS-14) Issue type, default Task
OpenProject API key (My account → Access tokens); SATOM sends the user name apikey Project id or identifier Type id, default 1 (Task)
Vikunja Bearer API token with at least Create on tasks Project id (the number in the project URL) —

On a change request, Raise change ticket via integration hooks then opens the ticket synchronously and writes its reference and link onto the change: "Opened in — ." A change that already carries a reference is sent as a re-request and never opens a second ticket. A failure is shown in red and recorded on the change's timeline; it never breaks the change itself.

Connect Confluence#

In the Confluence card fill New connection (name, Cloud or Data Center, https:// address, authentication, user and API token), Save, then Test: it says how many spaces the account sees. The token is write-only. The table lists each connection, whether its credential is stored, and how many Wiki pages it keeps up to date. Publishing — picking the space and the parent page — is done from the article: see Wiki → Confluence.

Write an integration hook#

  1. In Integration hooks (your Python) press New hook.
  2. Start from an example (optional): CRM change ticket (change.requested), Telegram, Slack or Microsoft Teams (all three on alert.fired). Picking one reloads the editor, so choose before you type. Each starter is a complete script: it calls its own run(ctx) when the hook fires and reports a non-2xx answer from the receiving system as a failed run.
  3. Fill in Slug (lowercase, digits and dashes — the directory name), Name, Event, Enabled, Timeout (s) (1–120, default 30) and Secrets this hook may read (comma separated), e.g. CRM_TOKEN.
  4. Write the code in hook.py and Save. "Saving compiles the source first — a syntax error is refused here, with its message, rather than discovered at 03:00 inside a maintenance window."
  5. Press Dry run with sample payload. The hook is queued against the event's sample payload through the same runner — the answer is queued; the outcome appears under Recent runs a moment later. A dry run also queues a disabled hook.

The runner executes hook.py as a script, top to bottom. Import the context from the SDK and do the work at module level (or call your function at the end):

from satom_sdk import ctx

p = ctx.payload
resp = ctx.http.post(
    "https://crm.example.com/api/changes",
    json={"title": p["title"], "starts_at": p.get("window_start")},
    headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + ctx.secret("CRM_TOKEN")},
)
if not resp.ok:
    ctx.result(False, {"detail": "CRM said %s" % resp.status})
else:
    ctx.log("opened %s" % resp.json().get("id"))
    ctx.result(True, {"id": resp.json().get("id")})

The hook sees ctx.payload, ctx.secret(NAME) (declared secrets only), ctx.http (get, post, put, patch, delete; every request has a forced timeout within the hook's budget; the response offers status, ok, text, json() and headers), ctx.log() and ctx.result(ok, data). The verdict comes only from ctx.result — printing JSON cannot fake it. A script that exits with code 0 without calling ctx.result is recorded as ok; a non-zero exit is failed.

The starters follow the same pattern: they define run(ctx) and end with an if __name__ == "__main__": block that imports ctx from satom_sdk and calls it. Keep that block if you rename or restructure the function.

ℹ️Note

Changed in 2.11.0: the starters run as saved (before, they did nothing and were still recorded as ok), a hook's crq_ref / crq_url is written onto the change request, and secret values are entered in the hook editor.

Set a hook's secret values#

  1. Declare the names under Secrets this hook may read and Save the hook.
  2. The Secret values card appears below the editor and lists each declared name as stored or not set.
  3. Pick the Secret, type the Value and press Store value. The flash reads "Secret stored. Its value is not shown again." Storing a name that already has a value replaces it.

Values are write-only: never shown, flashed or logged; the audit log records only the name and where it was stored (integration.secret.set). The card accepts only names the hook declares. Where a value is kept follows the mode under Settings → Vault, and the card says which: vault only keeps it only in the vault at <mount>/hooks/<NAME> (the database holds a marker), both adds an encrypted local copy as the fallback, and with no vault it is encrypted in the SATOM database. The runner reads each declared secret from the vault first, then from the local copy, then from the environment variable SATOM_HOOK_SECRET_<NAME> when it has no database. A declared secret with no value is missing from the hook's environment and ctx.secret() raises an error naming it; a secret the vault could not serve is recorded on the run as could not be read from the vault, with the reason.

Configuration#

Events#

Event Fires when Notes
change.requested You press Raise change ticket via integration hooks on a change Payload carries the change reference, devices by name, evidence per appliance, affected policies (first 500, with the true count), approval mode, existing ticket reference, window in UTC. A successful run whose result data carries crq_ref (and optionally crq_url) records that reference on the change
change.approved A change is approved in SATOM —
window.opening An authorised change starts running (moves to in progress) Fires on every start, whether or not NetBox is configured
window.closing A change's run finished and the change closed Fires whether or not NetBox is configured; outcome is the change's status (completed or failed)
upgrade.finished / upgrade.failed A change request closed as completed / failed One event per appliance on the change
alert.fired The health engine raised a finding that passed the Integration hooks sink filter Once per finding, only fresh out of cooldown, only from the writable primary; switch the sink on under Settings → Email & Alerts. Since 3.4.0 a device finding carries appliance_id, so a hook — or a process trigger — can address the device
intent.deviation The Intent deviation check found a bound appliance that no longer matches its template (see Alerting) Fires beside alert.fired for the same finding, under the same sink filter and cooldown. Payload: appliance, template, binding and the names of the fields that differ — never their values. Bind a hook to one of the two, not both, or it runs twice

The hook editor lists the exact payload fields and a sample for every event under Events SATOM emits.

ℹ️Note — Triggers are not a sink

A trigger on one of these events starts its automations inside SATOM — not through a hook, and not filtered by the Integration hooks sink; findings reach triggers straight from the health engine. In NAF terms hooks and triggers are two doors of the same Orchestrator block — see Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework.

NetBox and tracker fields#

Field Description Required Example
Base URL / URL Root URL of the service Yes https://netbox.example.com
API token Stored encrypted; blank keeps the existing one Yes (first save) —
Timeout (s) NetBox 1–60; tracker 3–60 No 10
Verify TLS Check the server certificate No ticked
Maintenance-window backend journal / tag / custom fields NetBox Journal entry
Project / type / account e-mail Per tracker backend (see table above) Tracker OPS

Example#

🧪Example — Post every critical alert to a Teams channel

Create a hook from the Microsoft Teams starter, bound to alert.fired, declaring TEAMS_WEBHOOK_URL, and save. In the Secret values card store the webhook URL under TEAMS_WEBHOOK_URL, then press Dry run with sample payload — the sample card appears in the channel and the run shows ok under Recent runs. Then switch the Integration hooks sink on in Settings → Email & Alerts with a filter for critical findings.

Result#

  • Saved settings, test results and hook saves/deletes/dry runs are written to the audit log (integrations.netbox.save, integrations.tracker.save, integrations.netbox.schedule, integrations.hook.save, integrations.hook.dry_run, integrations.hook.delete, integration.secret.set). Token and secret values are never logged.
  • On a change request, the External change record card shows the approval mode, the ticket, the NetBox window state (none requested, open, closed, error) and an Integration log.
  • Hook sources are kept with up to 20 previous versions; deleting a hook keeps its version history.

Troubleshooting#

The NetBox window state says "error"#

Possible causes — SATOM asked NetBox and it refused or did not answer. A device may still be shown in maintenance in NetBox. This is deliberately different from none requested.

Solution — read the Integration log on the change, fix the cause (token, custom fields, mapping), and use Retry maintenance window in NetBox before the run, or clear the window in NetBox by hand after it.

"NetBox does not document : those appliances will be skipped and reported by name, …"#

Solution — map the named appliances under Device mapping (device id or vm:<id>), or fix the names so they match exactly.

"The integration is enabled but did NOT open a ticket: …"#

Solution — press Test connection in the Issue tracker card; check the project key / id and the token's rights on that project.

"Nothing was sent: no tracker backend is configured in Settings -> Integrations and no enabled hook is bound to change.requested."#

Solution — configure a tracker backend, or enable a hook bound to change.requested, or type the reference by hand with Record on the change.

A hook's ticket reference never appears on the change#

Possible causes — the reference is recorded only when the hook is bound to change.requested, its run ends ok, and its ctx.result data carries a non-empty crq_ref. A crq_url that does not start with http:// or https:// is dropped (the reference is still recorded), and a change that is already closed is left untouched. The hook's run status says whether the reference was recorded and, if not, why.

Solution — check the hook's Recent runs; fix the result keys or the failure, or copy the reference and press Record on the change's External change record card.

A hook stays "queued" forever#

Possible causes — satom-integrations.path is not enabled on the node that served the request (each node only drains its own queue).

Solution — systemctl enable --now satom-integrations.path on that node; check with sudo satom get timer status.

Advanced#

Advanced The hook runner sandbox

Saving a hook writes it to data/integrations/hooks/<slug>/; nothing runs in the web application. A dispatch writes a request file into data/integrations/queue/; satom-integrations.path starts satom-integrations.service, which runs as the unprivileged satom user with a hardened systemd sandbox (read-only system, private /tmp, only the integrations directory writable). Each hook runs as python -E -s -B hook.py in a fresh temporary directory with an environment built from scratch — no database URL, no encryption key, no device credentials, only the declared secrets — and cannot import the application. A timeout kills the whole process group.

Since 2026-10-15 every hook also runs inside bubblewrap: private process, user, IPC and network namespaces, with only the system libraries, the Python environment (read-only), the resolver and CA files and the hook's own directory visible. Without that jail a hook — same system user as the web application — could open the SATOM database over its local socket and read the encryption key from another process. A node without bubblewrap refuses hooks instead of running them unconfined; install it from Settings → General → System packages.

Network goes through a proxy the runner serves for each hook. HTTP(S) (ctx.http, requests, httpx, urllib) uses it unchanged; for SSH or other TCP protocols use satom_sdk.tcp(host, port) and hand the socket over, e.g. paramiko.SSHClient().connect(host, sock=tcp(host, 22), …). The proxy refuses this node (loopback and every address it owns) and link-local addresses, checking the connected socket rather than the name, and every attempt is listed in the hook's run record. Captured output is redacted (declared secret values masked) and capped at 8 000 characters. At most 50 requests are drained per invocation; a claim older than 15 minutes is treated as a dead runner.

Advanced High availability

satom-integrations.path must be enabled on both nodes. A node whose watcher is disabled accepts queued work and never runs it. alert.fired is dispatched only by the writable primary.

Advanced Approval modes on a change request

Manual — approved in SATOM. External — fail-closed: the change is runnable only once an external approval timestamp is recorded on it; unreachable, slow and unanswered all count as not approved, and an edit of the window, risk or approval mode clears it. An integration records the verdict with POST /api/v1/change-requests/<id>/external-approval (admin-scope API token); an administrator can also record or withdraw it by hand on the change's External change record card; see Change requests.
